real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to sharp, close-up dog faces (and dog-like animals) that fill most of the frame. It is most active when the subject is large and in focus, centered, often cut off by the frame, and seen against a background with no visible horizon or straight lines. It responds less to small, blurry or left-facing subjects. The frontal and left/right facing effects are largely shared with similar units, so the rows chosen are the ones particular to this unit: sharpness, a subject filling more than three quarters of the photo, and the absence of straight lines.

real_s2.explanation: The unit responds most to dog (and dog-like) faces or bodies that fill the frame in sharp focus. It likes close-up, centered subjects facing the camera rather than in profile, and textured fur with no visible straight lines or horizon. Activity drops when the animal is small, blurry, off to the side, or shown in a scene with man-made straight lines. Several of these traits (frontal facing, large subject) are shared with similar units. What looks particular to this unit is sensitivity to sharpness, to a subject filling most of the frame, and to the absence of straight lines.

real_s3.explanation: The unit responds most to dogs (and dog-like animals such as wolves, dingoes and the lesser panda) that are large in the frame, in sharp focus, and seen close up. The background is plain or textured, with no visible horizon or straight lines. It is also biased toward subjects facing the camera rather than to the left, but the similar units share that bias. What sets it apart is a preference for sharp, frame-filling close-ups of fur and faces without structured scenery.
